metadata.title: A Measure of Asymptotic Efficiency for Tests of a Hypothesis Based on the Sum of Observations
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available (pre-arXiv classic). Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Asymptotic efficiency of a test based on $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^n X_j$
nodes.statement: Given a simple null $H_0$ vs.\ simple alternative $H_1$, consider tests that reject $H_0$ when $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^n X_j \le k$. Construct an index $\rho$ that, for a test specified by the chance variable $X$, captures asymptotic test efficiency, so that $e=\log\rho_1/\log\rho_2$ measures the relative efficiency of two such tests for large samples.
nodes.statement_clean: Define an asymptotic-efficiency index for tests that reject when the sum of observations falls below a threshold, and use it to compare two such tests.

nodes.name: Notation 1: $S_n$, $F$, $M$, $m(a)$
nodes.statement: $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^n X_j$ is the sum of $n$ i.i.d.\ copies of $X$ with moment generating function $M(t)=E(e^{tX})$ and CDF $F(x)=P(X\le x)$. Define $m(a)=\inf_t E(e^{t(X-a)}) = \inf_t e^{-ta}M(t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Notation: $m(a)$ is the infimum over $t$ of the moment generating function of $X-a$.

nodes.name: Lemma 1: $M(t)$ attains its minimum
nodes.statement: $M(t)$ attains its minimum value $m(0)$. The minimum is attained for finite $t$ unless $P(X>0)=0$ or $P(X<0)=0$; in that event $m(0)=P(X=0)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The MGF $M(t)$ attains its infimum, at finite $t$ except when $X$ is one-signed.
assumptions: $X$ is a chance variable with MGF $M(t)=E(e^{tX})$
conclusions: If $P(X>0)>0$ and $P(X<0)>0$, the minimum is attained at some finite $t$

nodes.name: Lemma 2: positivity of $m(0)$
nodes.statement: If $P(X\le 0)>0$ and $P(X\ge 0)>0$, then $m(0)>0$.
nodes.statement_clean: When $X$ takes values of both signs (allowing zero), $m(0)$ is strictly positive.

nodes.name: Lemma 3: derivatives of $M(t)$
nodes.statement: For all $t$ in the interior of the interval where $M(t)$ is finite, $dM/dt=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x e^{tx} dF(x)$ and $d^2M/dt^2=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 e^{tx} dF(x)\ge 0$, with $d^2M/dt^2=0$ iff $P(X=0)=1$.
nodes.statement_clean: Derivatives of $M(t)$ may be obtained by differentiation under the integral sign; $M$ is convex.
assumptions: $t$ lies in the interior of the interval where $M(t)$ is finite

nodes.name: Lemma 4: interchange of $\lim$ and $\inf$
nodes.statement: If $u_1(t),u_2(t),\dots$ is a nondecreasing sequence of functions continuous on $[a,b]$, then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{a\le t\le b} u_n(t) = \inf_{a\le t\le b}\lim_{n\to\infty} u_n(t)$. Extends to $\infty$-valued $u_n$ and to $a=-\infty$ provided $u_n(-\infty)=\lim_{t\to -\infty} u_n(t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: For monotone nondecreasing sequences of continuous functions, the limit of the infima equals the infimum of the limit (Lebesgue–monotone convergence on intervals).
nodes.origin_citation: Saks, Theory of the Integral, 2nd ed., 1937

nodes.name: Theorem 1: large-deviation bound $P(S_n\le na)\le m(a)^n$
nodes.statement: If $E(X)>-\infty$ and $a\le E(X)$, then $P(S_n\le na)\le [m(a)]^n$. Symmetrically, if $E(X)<+\infty$ and $a\ge E(X)$, then $P(S_n\ge na)\le [m(a)]^n$. Moreover the bound is tight: for $0<\epsilon<m(a)$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}(m(a)-\epsilon)^n / P(S_n\le na) = 0$ (and similarly for the upper tail).
nodes.statement_clean: Chernoff bound: the tail probability of a sum of i.i.d.\ variables decays at exactly the exponential rate $m(a)^n$.
assumptions: $E(X)>-\infty$ and $a\le E(X)$ (lower tail) / $E(X)<+\infty$ and $a\ge E(X)$ (upper tail)
nodes.notes: This is what came to be known as the Chernoff bound; the paper notes that Cramér [1] obtained related results under stronger hypotheses (existence of MGF on a two-sided interval and absolutely continuous CDF).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Upper bound by Markov on $e^{tS_n}$ for $t\le 0$; matching lower bound by reduction to a discrete distribution and a multinomial-counting / Stirling argument, then approximation of general $X$ by discretizations $X^{(s)}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Upper bound from MGF/Markov; lower bound by an explicit multinomial construction matching $m(a)$ and a discretization step for general distributions.

nodes.name: Upper bound via extended Tchebycheff inequality
nodes.statement: By the extended Tchebycheff inequality, $E(e^{tS_n})=[M(t)]^n \ge P(S_n\le 0)$ for $t\le 0$. Hence $P(S_n\le 0)\le [\inf_{t\le 0} M(t)]^n$, and $a\le E(X)$ implies $\inf_{t\le 0} M(t)=\inf_t M(t)=m(0)$, giving (3.5).

nodes.name: Discrete case: multinomial lower bound
nodes.statement: Reduce (3.7) to $a=0$. Treat the discrete case $P(X=x_i)=p_i$: pick finite $r$ so $m^* = \sum_{i=1}^r e^{t^* x_i} p_i > \inf_t\sum_{i=1}^\infty e^{tx_i}p_i - \epsilon/2$, then exhibit positive integers $n_1,\dots,n_r$ with $\sum n_i=n$, $\sum n_i x_i\le 0$ such that the multinomial probability $P(n_1,\dots,n_r)= n!\prod p_i^{n_i}/\prod n_i! > (m^*-\epsilon/2)^n$.

nodes.name: Stirling + Lagrange-multiplier optimization
nodes.statement: Stirling gives $P(n_1,\dots,n_r)\ge \{\prod_{i=1}^r (np_i/n_i)^{n_i}\}\cdot n^{-r/2}$. Maximizing $Q(n_1,\dots,n_r)=\prod (np_i/n_i)^{n_i}$ subject to $\sum n_i=n$, $\sum n_i x_i=0$, $n_i>0$ via Lagrange multipliers yields $(m^*)^n$ at $n_i^{(0)}=np_i e^{t^*x_i}/m^*$.

nodes.name: Discretization for general $X$
nodes.statement: For general $X$, define $X^{(s)}=i/s$ when $(i-1)/s<X\le i/s$. Then $P(S_n\le 0)\ge P(S_n^{(s)}\le 0)$ and $M^{(s)}(t)\ge e^{-|t|/s} M(t)$, so $\inf M^{(s)}(t)\ge \inf M(t)-\epsilon/2$ for $s$ large; the result follows from the discrete case.

nodes.name: Notation 2: $a_e$ and $t(a)$
nodes.statement: Let $a_e$ be defined by $P(X<a_e)=0$ and $P(X<a_e+\epsilon)>0$ for every $\epsilon>0$. Let $t(a)$ be given by $m(a)=e^{-a t(a)} M[t(a)]$.
nodes.statement_clean: $a_e$ is the essential left endpoint of $X$; $t(a)$ is the minimizing argument $t$ in the definition of $m(a)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5: degenerate / one-sided case
nodes.statement: If $E(X)>-\infty$ and $M(t)=\infty$ for $t<0$, then $t(a)=0$ and $m(a)=1$ for $a\le E(X)$.
nodes.statement_clean: When the MGF blows up on the negative axis, the optimum lies at $t=0$ and $m(a)\equiv 1$ on $a\le E(X)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 6: properties of $m(a)$ near $a_e$
nodes.statement: If $M(t)<\infty$ for some $t<0$, then $E(X)>-\infty$, and $m(a)=0$ for $a<a_e$, $m(a_e)=P(X=a_e)$, and $m[E(X)]=1$. Furthermore, $m(a)$ is continuous and strictly monotone increasing on $a_e\le a\le E(X)$.
nodes.statement_clean: When the MGF is finite somewhere on the negative axis, $m(a)$ is continuous, strictly increasing on $[a_e, E(X)]$, with boundary values $m(a_e)=P(X=a_e)$ and $m(E(X))=1$.
conclusions: $m(a)$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $a_e\le a\le E(X)$

nodes.name: Notation 3: index $\rho$ of a test
nodes.statement: $H_0,H_1$ specify distributions with $\mu_0=E(X|H_0)\le\mu_1=E(X|H_1)$; the test rejects $H_0$ when $S_n>na$, with $\alpha=P(S_n>na|H_0)$ and $\beta=P(S_n\le na|H_1)$. Let $\rho(a)=\max[m_0(a),m_1(a)]$ where $m_i(a)=\inf_t E(e^{t(X-a)}|H_i)$. The index of the test determined by $X$ is $\rho=\inf_{\mu_0\le a\le \mu_1}\rho(a)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The asymptotic-efficiency index $\rho$ of a test minimizes over $a\in[\mu_0,\mu_1]$ the worst-case exponential rate $\max(m_0(a),m_1(a))$.

nodes.name: Theorem 2: $\rho$ governs $\inf_a(\beta+\lambda\alpha)$
nodes.statement: Given $\epsilon>0$ and $\lambda$ with $0<\lambda<\infty$: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\{\inf_a (\beta+\lambda\alpha)/(\rho+\epsilon)^n\}=0$, and for $0<\epsilon<\rho$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\{\inf_a (\beta+\lambda\alpha)/(\rho-\epsilon)^n\}=\infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: The minimum over $a$ of $\beta+\lambda\alpha$ decays exactly like $\rho^n$, so $\rho$ is the right asymptotic-efficiency index.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Pick $a_0$ with $\rho(a_0)\le\rho+\epsilon/2$ and apply Theorem 1 to obtain (4.21). For (4.22), exhibit $a_2\in[\mu_0,\mu_1]$ with $m_0(a_2),m_1(a_2)\ge\rho$ using continuity / monotonicity of $m_i$ from Lemma 6, then bound $\beta+\lambda\alpha\ge\lambda P(S_n\ge na_1|H_0)$ and apply the lower-bound part of Theorem 1.

nodes.name: Notation 4: relative efficiency $e=\log\rho_1/\log\rho_2$
nodes.statement: For two tests $T_1,T_2$ with indices $\rho_1,\rho_2$, define the asymptotic relative efficiency by $e=\log\rho_1/\log\rho_2$ (undefined if $\rho_1=\rho_2=1$). For $T_i$, $\gamma_i=\inf_a(\beta+\lambda\alpha)$ is a function of $n_i$ and $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_clean: The asymptotic relative efficiency $e$ of $T_1$ to $T_2$ is the ratio $\log\rho_1/\log\rho_2$ of their indices.

nodes.name: Theorem 3: efficiency interpretation of $e$
nodes.statement: If $\lim n_2/n_1<e$ ($>e$), then $\lim_{n_1,n_2\to\infty} \gamma_1/\gamma_2=\infty$ ($=0$). $e$ does not depend on $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_clean: The ratio $e=\log\rho_1/\log\rho_2$ measures sample-size efficiency: $T_1$ on $n_1$ observations matches $T_2$ on $n_2 \approx e\, n_1$ observations.
assumptions: $\lim n_2/n_1$ exists and is compared with $e=\log\rho_1/\log\rho_2$
nodes.notes: Stated as an immediate consequence of Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Example 1: Normal $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)$
nodes.statement: If $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)$ under $H_i$ ($\mu_0<\mu_1$): $e^{-at}M_i(t)=e^{(\mu_i-a)t+\frac{1}{2}\sigma_i^2 t^2}$, $m_i(a)=e^{\frac{1}{2}(\mu_i-a)^2/\sigma_i^2}$, and $\rho=\rho\bigl(\frac{\sigma_1\mu_0+\sigma_0\mu_1}{\sigma_1+\sigma_0}\bigr)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}[(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2}$.
nodes.statement_clean: For Gaussian $X$, the index $\rho$ has a closed form involving $((\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0))^2$.

nodes.name: Example 2: Chi-square $X/\sigma_i^2\sim\chi^2_r$
nodes.statement: If $X/\sigma_i^2\sim\chi^2_r$ under $H_i$ ($\sigma_0^2<\sigma_1^2$): $e^{-at}M_i(t)=e^{-at}(1-2\sigma_i^2 t)^{-r/2}$, $\log m_i(a)=-\tfrac{1}{2}[a/\sigma_i^2 + r\log(r\sigma_i^2/a) - r]$, and $\log\rho=-\tfrac{r}{2}[\delta-1-\log\delta]$ with $\delta=(\log\tau)/(\tau-1)$, $\tau=\sigma_0^2/\sigma_1^2$. As $\tau\to 1$, $\log\rho\approx -r(\tau-1)^2/16$.
nodes.statement_clean: For chi-square $X$, $\log\rho$ has a closed form in $\tau=\sigma_0^2/\sigma_1^2$.

nodes.name: Example 3: Binomial $X\sim B(r,p_i)$
nodes.statement: If $X\sim B(r,p_i)$ under $H_i$ ($p_0<p_1$): $e^{-at}M_i(t)=e^{-at}(p_ie^t+q_i)^r$, $\log m_i(a)=(r-a)\log[rq_i/(r-a)]+a\log[rp_i/a]$, and $\log\rho=r\{(1-c)\log[q_0/(1-c)]+c\log[p_0/c]\}$ where $c=\log(q_0/q_1)/[\log(q_0/q_1)+\log(p_1/p_0)]$. As $p_1\to p_0$, $\log\rho\approx -r(p_1-p_0)^2/(8 p_0 q_0)$.
nodes.statement_clean: For binomial $X$, $\log\rho$ has a closed form involving $c=\log(q_0/q_1)/(\log(q_0/q_1)+\log(p_1/p_0))$.

nodes.name: Notation 5: $N(t),P(t),t_0,a_0$
nodes.statement: Let $N(t)=E(Xe^{tX})$, $P(t)=E(X^2 e^{tX})$, $t_0=\mathrm{glb}\{t:M(t)<\infty\}$, and for $t_0<t<0$ let $a_0=\inf_{t_0<t<0} N(t)/M(t)$. If $E(X)>-\infty$ then $a_e<E(X)$ except when $P(X=a_e)=1$; if $a_e>-\infty$ then $t_0=-\infty$.
nodes.statement_clean: Auxiliary expectations and the lower edge of the MGF’s domain of finiteness.

nodes.name: Notation 6: log-likelihood-ratio variable $X$
nodes.statement:
An experiment outcome $Y$ has density $f_i$ under $H_i$ via $
u_i(E)=\int_E f_i d
u$ for $
u=(
u_0+
u_1)/2$. The log-likelihood ratio is $X=\log f_1(Y)-\log f_0(Y)$. Set $M_i(t)=E(e^{tX}|H_i)$, $N_i(t)=E(Xe^{tX}|H_i)$, $P_i(t)=E(X^2 e^{tX}|H_i)$, with $m_i(a),t_i(a)$ the corresponding $m,t$ functions under $H_i$.
nodes.statement_clean: Definition of the log-likelihood ratio statistic $X$ and its conditional MGF/derivatives under each hypothesis.

nodes.name: Lemma 7: derivative identities for $m(a)$, $t(a)$
nodes.statement: If $M(t)<\infty$ for some $t<0$ and $a_e<E(X)$, then for $a_0<a<E(X)$: $a=N(t(a))/M(t(a))$, $d[\log m(a)]/da=-t(a)$, and $dt(a)/da=M(t)^2/[M(t)P(t)-N(t)^2]_{t=t(a)}>0$. If finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ exist, the same hold for $a_0<a\le E(X)$, with $d\log m(a)/da|_{a=\mu}=0$ and $dt(a)/da|_{a=\mu}=1/\sigma^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: Differential identities relating $m(a)$, $t(a)$ and the conditional moments through the MGF.

nodes.name: Lemma 8: index of the likelihood-ratio test
nodes.statement: If $X$ is the log-likelihood ratio, $X\not\equiv 0$, and $X$ is finite with probability one, then $M_1(t)=M_0(t+1)$ and $N_1(t)=N_0(t+1)$. As $a$ varies from $\mu_0$ to $\mu_1$, $t_0(a)$ varies continuously from $0$ to $1$, $t_0(a)=t_1(a)+1$, and $\rho=\inf_{0<t<1} M_0(t) = \inf_{0<t<1}\int [f_1(x)]^t [f_0(x)]^{1-t} d\nu(x)$.
nodes.statement_clean: For likelihood-ratio tests, $\rho$ equals the infimum over $t\in(0,1)$ of $\int f_1^t f_0^{1-t}\,d\nu$ (the Chernoff information / Rényi-divergence formula).
nodes.notes: Equation (6.24) is the Chernoff information formula now standard in information theory.

nodes.name: Theorem 4: normal approximation of $\rho$ for likelihood-ratio tests
nodes.statement: If for a class $C$ of likelihood-ratio tests $M_0(t)=1+\mu_0 t+(\mu_0^2+\sigma_0^2)t^2/2+o(\mu_0^2+\sigma_0^2)$ for $0<t<1$ and $M_1(t)=1+\mu_1 t+(\mu_1^2+\sigma_1^2)t^2/2+o(\mu_0^2+\sigma_0^2)$ for $-1<t<0$, then $\mu_1=\sigma_0^2/2+o(\sigma_0^2)$, $\mu_0=-\sigma_0^2/2+o(\sigma_0^2)$, $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_0^2+o(\sigma_0^2)$, and $\rho=e^{-\sigma_0^2/8}+o(\sigma_0^2)=e^{\mu_0/4}+o(\mu_0) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}[(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2}+o([(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2)$.
nodes.statement_clean: When the log-likelihood-ratio MGFs are well approximated by their second-order Taylor expansions, $\rho$ is approximated by the Gaussian formula from Example 1.
assumptions: Second-order MGF expansions for $M_0,M_1$ hold uniformly on the relevant intervals
conclusions: $\rho\approx e^{-\sigma_0^2/8}\approx e^{\mu_0/4}\approx e^{-\frac{1}{2}[(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2}$ to the stated order

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Part 1: From Lemma 8 ($M_1(t-1)=M_0(t)$ on $0<t<1$) match Taylor coefficients of the two expansions to obtain $\mu_1^2+\sigma_1^2=\mu_0^2+\sigma_0^2+o(\cdot)$, $\mu_1=\sigma_1^2/2+o(\cdot)$, $\mu_0=\sigma_1^2/2+o(\cdot)$. Part 2: $\rho=\inf_{0<t<1} M_0(t)$; minimizing the quadratic approximation gives $\rho=1-\mu_0^2/[2(\mu_0^2+\sigma_0^2)]+o(\mu_0^2+\sigma_0^2)$, then substitute Part 1.

nodes.name: Theorem 5: normal approximation for general $S_n$ tests with $X$ less efficient than the LR
nodes.statement: If for a class $C^*$ of tests $\sigma_i^2 dt_i(a)/da = 1+o(1)$ as $\mu_1-\mu_0\to 0$ for $\mu_0<a<\mu_1$, $i=0,1$, then $\rho = e^{-\frac{1}{2}[(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2} + o\bigl(\frac{\mu_1-\mu_0}{\sigma_1+\sigma_0}\bigr)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Under a mild regularity condition, $\rho$ for a general statistic-based test is approximated by the Gaussian formula when the hypotheses are close.
assumptions: For a class $C^*$ of tests, $\sigma_i^2 dt_i(a)/da=1+o(1)$ as $\mu_1-\mu_0\to 0$ for $\mu_0<a<\mu_1$, $i=0,1$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: Use $\log m_0(a)=-(a-\mu_0)^2/(2)\,[1/\sigma_0^2+o(1/\sigma_0^2)]$ and similarly for $\log m_1(a)$. Equate the main terms to get $\log\rho=-\tfrac{1}{2}[(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2+o([(\mu_1-\mu_0)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)]^2)$; the optimum is at $a\approx(\sigma_1\mu_0+\sigma_0\mu_1)/(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)$.

nodes.name: Information and divergence interpretation
nodes.statement: Define $I(X)=-\log\rho$, the information per observation; for the likelihood-ratio test, $D(Y)=-\log[\inf_{0<t<1}\int f_1^t f_0^{1-t} d\nu]$ is a divergence. Independent observations satisfy $D(Y_1,Y_2)\le D(Y_1)+D(Y_2)$, with $D(Y,Y)=2D(Y)$. The Kullback–Leibler measure achieves equality in $D(Y_1,Y_2)\le D(Y_1)+D(Y_2)$; the two divergences correspond to two distinct functionals of the type-1/type-2 error tradeoff curve.
nodes.statement_clean: $-\log\rho$ may be interpreted as information per observation; the resulting divergence differs from the Kullback–Leibler divergence but both arise from the type-1/type-2 error curve.

nodes.name: Definition of $m(a)$
nodes.statement: $m(a) = \inf_t E(e^{t(X-a)}) = \inf_t e^{-ta} M(t)$

nodes.name: Chernoff bound
nodes.statement: $P(S_n \le na) \le [m(a)]^n$ for $a\le E(X)$

nodes.name: Index $\rho$
nodes.statement: $\rho = \inf_{\mu_0\le a\le \mu_1} \max[m_0(a), m_1(a)]$

nodes.name: Cramér large-deviation theorem (cited)
nodes.statement: Under the assumption that $M(t)$ exists on some open interval $-A<t<A$ and $F$ is absolutely continuous, $P(S_n\le na)$ behaves roughly like $m(a)^n$ for $a<E(X)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Cramér’s precursor large-deviation result, requiring two-sided MGF and absolute continuity of $F$.
nodes.origin_citation: H. Cramér, “Sus un nouveau théorème-limite de la théorie des probabilités”, Actualités Scientifiques et Industrielles, No. 736, Paris 1938

nodes.name: Esseen normal-approximation bound (cited)
nodes.statement: Esseen's bound on the error of the normal approximation to the distribution of $S_n$ requires only the (finite) existence of third moments.
nodes.origin_citation: C. G. Esseen, “Fourier analysis of distribution functions”, Acta Math., 77 (1945) 1–125

nodes.name: Extended Tchebycheff inequality (cited)
nodes.statement: $E(e^{tS_n}) = [M(t)]^n \ge P(S_n\le 0)$ for $t\le 0$ (and the symmetric upper-tail version).

nodes.name: Kullback–Leibler divergence (cited)
nodes.statement: Kullback and Leibler defined a measure of divergence yielding equality in the additivity relation for independent observations.
nodes.origin_citation: Kullback & Leibler, “On information and sufficiency”, Ann. Math. Stat. 22 (1951) 79–86; Jeffreys, Theory of Probability, 2nd ed. 1948
